title: Machiavelli: The Prince
note: Machiavelli, a Florentine diplomat, wrote The Prince about 1513 as practical advice on gaining and keeping power. He judged actions by their results, urged rulers to rely on their own arms, and set virtù (ability and drive) against fortuna (chance). Quotations follow W. K. Marriott's translation.

read.title: Fortune and the flood
text: From Chapter XXV, “What Fortune Can Effect in Human Affairs and How to Withstand Her”:

Nevertheless, not to extinguish our free will, I hold it to be true that Fortune is the arbiter of one-half of our actions, but that she still leaves us to direct the other half, or perhaps a little less.

I compare her to one of those raging rivers, which when in flood overflows the plains, sweeping away trees and buildings, bearing away the soil from place to place; everything flies before it, all yield to its violence, without being able in any way to withstand it; and yet, though its nature be such, it does not follow therefore that men, when the weather becomes fair, shall not make provision, both with defences and barriers, in such a manner that, rising again, the waters may pass away by canal, and their force be neither so unrestrained nor so dangerous. So it happens with fortune, who shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her, and thither she turns her forces where she knows that barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her.

q.q: How much of our actions does Machiavelli leave to fortune?
o: About half; we direct the rest, or a little less
None, since free will governs all

q.q: What should people do when the weather is fair?
o: Enjoy it, since floods cannot be resisted
Build defenses and barriers so the flood does less harm

q.q: Where does fortune show her power, according to the passage?
o: Where valour has not prepared to resist her
